$comment: The machine-readable half of docs/wpt-plan.md. That document is the argument; this is the
state. One entry per task as that document numbers them.
status: not_started | in_progress | done | refused
in_progress means an agent has claimed it. Claim by setting status and `agent`, committing
that change ALONE, and pushing before starting. A conflict on a one-line commit is the
cheapest possible collision.
done means `check` was RUN and PASSED, and the run is quoted in the commit message.
refused means an ADR says this browser will not do it. `notes` names the ADR.
`scope` is a one-line reminder, not the specification. The specification is the named section
of docs/wpt-plan.md plus the ADR in `adr`. Do not expand `scope` into a copy of the plan; two
copies diverge and then neither is true.
`target` is a subtest pass rate in the named WPT path, as microbrowser_wpt reports it. It is a
planning number, not a contract: an area that turns out to be mostly deliberate deviation gets
its target revised HERE and in the plan, with the reason.
`firefox_ceiling` is Firefox's pass rate on the same tests, from wpt.fyi. This is the data-
driven upper bound: a gap between us and the ceiling is a bug; a test Firefox also fails is
not our problem yet. Regenerated by `tools/wpt/firefox-ref.py`.
`ceiling_source` is `firefox` when the ceiling comes from a wpt.fyi measurement, or
`refused:ADR-NNNN` when an ADR says this browser will not implement the area.
`firefox_gap` is written by tools/wpt/firefox-gap.py --annotate-tasks and is the ranking: test
files Firefox passes and this browser does not, for the task's `area`. Rank by
firefox_gap.files. A subtest percentage is NOT the ranking and is not comparable across areas
or across browsers -- its denominator is the subtests we managed to report.
`firefox_gap_unblocks` is for a task with no `area` of its own, which would otherwise sort as
zero. It is what the task makes reachable elsewhere, and it is ranked against firefox_gap.files.
`claimed` is the date an agent took the task, and `stale_claim` is an audit of one that was
never released. See docs/wpt-plan.md s0, Claiming a task, for when a claim may be re-taken.

tasks.title: the server's built-in handlers
tasks.scope: WPT's `.py` handlers, as a table of native handlers in tools/wpt/Server.cpp. Not a Python interpreter -- ADR 0040 rules that out and is right. The head of the distribution is short and mechanical: slow.py, stash.py, redirect.py, serve-custom-response.py, report.py, content.py, serve-with-content-type.py, message.py, inspect-headers.py, cors-makeheader.py, status.py, echo-headers.py. POST is also refused outright today -- Server.cpp answers 501 for any method that is not GET or HEAD -- which blocks every xhr/ and fetch/ test that sends one, whatever the handler.
tasks.check: xhr/ and fetch/api/ re-measured, with the `Python handlers are not implemented` cause gone from the ranked-cause table in docs/wpt-baseline.md.
tasks.notes:
**Measured 2026-08-12, and unclaimed until then: 2,214 in-scope test files reference a `.py` handler** -- 976 css/, 434 html/, 203 xhr/, 171 fetch/, 88 content-security-policy/, 57 eventsource/, 57 referrer-policy/. 308 distinct handlers, but the head is short (slow.py 216 references, stash.py 199, redirect.py 182). This is the only large blocker in the tree that is **entirely our own code** and needs no browser feature at all, which probably makes it the cheapest points available. Found by re-running a 599-test sample of the harness-failure bucket against the current tree: 26 of them reported `Error: Python handlers are not implemented`.

**2026-08-12, first 21 handlers landed**, plus POST (the server framed a request at the blank line and read the entity as the next request line, so it could not have answered one). xhr 135 -> 120 harness failures, cors 7 -> 8, fetch 204 -> 192; 672 recorded subtest failures became passes. The handlers immediately found a *browser* bug: a response to HEAD carries no body whatever its Content-Length says (RFC 9110 s6.4.1), and `net::ResponseParser` waited for one -- every HEAD request hung the browser forever. Still to do: `slow.py`, `delay.py` and `trickle.py` answer immediately, because the server is single-threaded and sleeping in it stops the whole run; a real delay wants a timer queue rather than a sleep. And 287 handlers remain unwritten -- the ranked-cause table in docs/wpt-baseline.md is how the next one gets chosen, which is why an unknown handler is still an honest 501.

**2026-08-12, second landing: nine more handlers, and the instrument that picks the next one.** The ranking this task was being worked from is wrong -- `Handlers.h` ranks missing handlers by how many files *name* them, and the top three of that list (`gentest.py` 3,766 files, `generate.py` 2,085, `build-compute-kind-widget-fallback-props.py` 802) are the generator scripts that produced the tests and are never fetched. `MICROBROWSER_WPT_HANDLER_REPORT=1` now records what was actually requested; use it, not grep. Over xhr/+fetch/+cors/ it found 79 handlers requested 2,877 times, headed by `dispatcher.py` at 1,091, which the grep list does not mention at all.

Landed: dispatcher, record-headers, image, content-length, corsenabled, status-code (both copies), nosniff, expose-headers, method. Unimplemented handler *requests* 2,877 -> 1,609. Harness-level failures 267 -> 260. **Subtest net is flat (162 newly passing, 159 newly failing) and that is the expected shape** -- a handler that answers lets a test run further, so subtests that never executed now execute and some fail. Judge this work by the harness column and the request count.

**Two things to know before continuing.** A handler is dispatched by file *name* and ten of the twenty-one original names have several distinct implementations in the checkout (`redirect.py`: eight files, eight bodies) -- TD-0061, with the audit table and why it must be fixed one copy at a time rather than blanket-scoped. And `tools/wpt/Handlers.cpp` is now compiled into `microbrowser_tests`, so a transcription is checkable in milliseconds instead of a suite run; add a test with each handler.

Next by request count: `stale-script.py` (806 -- grew from 401 because tests get further now), `http-cache.py` (140), `cache.py` (103), `clear-site-data.py` (91), `header-link.py` (74).

**Triaged 2026-08-12, after `record-headers.py` landed, and the answer is that handlers are done here.** `fetch/metadata/` is 87 tests and 1,664 subtests at 4.0%, and its handler is now implemented -- the report for that directory is down to `header-link.py` (74 requests) and nothing else that matters. What blocks the 87 is **three features, none of them a handler**:

1. **`window.open()`** returns null, so every generated `element-*.sub.html` fails at `win.document.createElement` with `cannot read property 'document' of null`. `induceRequest` opens a window and builds the element *in it* -- there is no variant that does not. Task J6, and it wants the realm (ADR 0042 §5) underneath it.
2. **An HTTPS origin.** `helper.sub.js` builds its origins from `{{ports[https][0]}}`, and this server binds HTTP only, so every "HTTPS upgrade", "HTTPS downgrade" and "non-trustworthy" subtest is unreachable. Task H9.
3. **`Sec-Fetch-*` request headers**, which this browser never sends -- `grep -rn Sec-Fetch src/` is empty. That is what the tests actually assert on, so it is the last of the three rather than the first: it gains nothing until 1 and 2 land, because the assertions are not reached.

**So do not spend more handler effort on this directory.** The same check applies elsewhere: `stale-script.py` is 806 requests and only **6 tests** (`fetch/stale-while-revalidate/`), because the tests poll -- so request count is not value either, and the directory size is the number to look at before committing to a handler.

**Claim audited 2026-08-17 and found stale** -- no claim commit; the handler work landed across 2026-08-12..14 and its own notes say the directory it was aimed at is done with handlers. Under the rule in docs/wpt-plan.md s0 (Claiming a task) this may be re-taken; say so in the claiming commit. The work already landed is in the git log and in the notes above; what is left is what the `check` field still asks for.

tasks.title: testdriver.js: how a test synthesises input
tasks.scope: 1,158 in-scope tests load testdriver.js and get `not implemented by testdriver-vendor.js`. This browser has an input path -- microbrowser_snapshot -click already drives it -- and no way for a page to reach it. Decide the seam, as ADR 0040 s3 decided the one for results.
tasks.check: ADR 0040 says what testdriver.js resolves to, and dom/events/ no longer reports action_sequence() as its top cause. Run 2026-08-14: on a 150-file sample of the tests that load testdriver.js, 2,244 subtests are counted with 247 passing and **zero** `not implemented by testdriver-vendor.js` anywhere in the run. uievents/click/click_events_on_input.html TIMEOUT -> OK.
tasks.notes:
Found by B3. Not a browser bug: the seam exists, nothing exposes it. The answer wants the same shape as the report seam -- a harness-only global reached through EvaluateScript, absent from a normal process.

**Done 2026-08-14, and B3's prediction of the shape was exactly right.** `tools/wpt/harness/testdriver-vendor.js` queues a tab-separated line on a global; the runner drains it in the poll that already asks whether the page has finished, and drives the **real** `ipc::PointerInputMessage` and `ipc::KeyInputMessage`. It has to be the real path: ADR 0017 makes a page's own synthetic event untrusted, so a `test_driver.click()` implemented as `element.click()` would pass the half of a test that counts handler calls and fail the half that checks what the click did.

`click` is move-down-up because a page listening on `pointerdown` is ordinary. `send_keys` focuses from the page first, which is what WebDriver's own Element Send Keys does. `action_sequence` covers pointer move/down/up, key down/up and pause, and rejects anything else rather than approximating it.

**It immediately found a real bug**: `element.click()` produced a *trusted* event, and a test in tests/ asserted that it did. Fixed in the same session.

**Partly done 2026-08-17, and it stays in_progress: the state file covers 134 of the 297 areas.** `tests/wpt/summary-state.tsv` is committed and is real -- 4,650 tests, 1,252,795 subtests, 1,223,991 passing -- from 20 of 93 shards. What is left is machine time and nothing else: `tools/wpt/baseline.sh` runs the rest, skips what the state already covers (it derives that from the state file itself, so a later session or another machine can pick it up), and stops on a runner failure rather than writing a state with a hole in it.

**The cost is timeouts and it is five to six hours, not the 'better part of a day' this task assumed.** Measured: 6,934 of the 23,146 testharness files are expected to TIMEOUT and 2,807 carry a `timeout=long` meta, which is a 65-second budget each; at the default --jobs that is ~2.75s of wall clock per expected timeout. `content-security-policy/` alone is 1,637s (869 tests, 278 of them long). Everything else is fast -- `dom/` 692 tests in 214s, `encoding/` 1,293 in 272s. Do **not** raise --jobs to close the gap: tools/wpt/main.cpp has the measurement showing it deletes subtests from CPU-bound areas.

**Two tooling bugs found and fixed, both in the path this task depends on.** `summary.Add` was gated on `--summary` alone, so `--summary-state FILE <area>` ran the area, printed "summary state written", and wrote a file of three comment lines -- verified against the pre-fix binary. The same bug had been found once before one line lower down (the *save* inside the `--summary` branch); fixing the save and leaving the feed is why it read as fixed for three days. And the write guard counted every `| ` row in docs/wpt-baseline.md rather than its `## Per area` section, so it read 301 against a 297-row table and would have refused a complete run on four hand-merged preamble rows it wrote itself. tests/WptSummaryTests.cpp is the first test of any of this.

**Found on the way, and it is a browser bug rather than this task's:** `content-security-policy/inheritance/inheritance-from-initiator.sub.html` **segfaults in all three of its variants** (`?scheme=javascript`, `?scheme=blob`, `?scheme=data`), deterministically, in 3.2 seconds -- `microbrowser_wpt --retries 0 <that path>`. All three are expected OK, so they either regressed or were never run. `content-security-policy/reporting/report-uri-from-child-frame.html` crashes too. Both are frame-shaped, which is where ADR 0042 §5's use-after-free lived.

The check has not been run: with 134 of 297 areas the writer refuses to regenerate the document, and printed exactly that -- "docs/wpt-baseline.md already describes 297 areas and this run has 134". That refusal is the guard working; finish the shards and it goes away.

tasks.title: dom/nodes
tasks.scope: Mutation algorithms, node comparison, adoption, ownerDocument.
tasks.check: dom/nodes/ >= 85%. Run 2026-08-11 (mutation algorithms): 3389 of 5451 subtests (62.2%) -> 3567 of 5529 (64.5%), dom/ as a whole 3850 of 7098 (54.2%) -> 4025 of 7176 (56.1%), 0 regressions across dom/, shadow-dom/, custom-elements/, domparsing/ and html/dom/. Not yet 85%, and the remainder is measured -- see notes.
tasks.notes:
**Third pass landed 2026-08-11: the mutation algorithms and the records they queue.** `dom/nodes` 62.2% -> **64.5%**, `dom/` 54.2% -> **56.1%**, 0 regressions.

**The finding is a hang reachable from any page.** `el.append(el)` built a *cycle* in the tree, so every walk from the root looped forever -- three files in dom/nodes ran the runner to its wall-clock budget and reported no subtest at all, which is why ranking an area by failing subtests never showed them. `append`, `prepend`, `replaceChildren`, `before`, `after` and `replaceWith` inserted their arguments one at a time and validated nothing, while appendChild/insertBefore/replaceChild had been validated since C1. All six now begin with the DOM's "converting nodes into a node" (S4.2.6) and end in a pre-insertion, which is also what makes them atomic: `doc.append(a, b)` on a document that already has an element throws and changes nothing. src/bindings/NodeMixins.cpp (new) is the six of them, split out because TreeMutation.cpp went past the module's line cap and because they are one specification section rather than six methods; PreInsertionError moved to BindingSupport.h so both translation units can ask it.

**MutationObserver was failing on a field it never wrote, and that hid six whole files.** Every MutationObserver test in dom/nodes runs through mutationobservers.js, which compares all eight record fields against a default of null; records carried no previousSibling, nextSibling or attributeNamespace, so each file failed on "previousSibling didn't match" before reaching its subject and then hung to the harness timeout waiting on an async_test that could no longer finish. 42 subtests in MutationObserver-attributes alone, 0 passing. The two siblings are computed inside RecordMutation rather than passed in, because every caller is already standing at the one moment they are true: an insertion records after the nodes are in, a removal before they leave. Landing with them: a replacement is now **one** record carrying addedNodes and removedNodes (the DOM's "suppress observers" flag, threaded as a bool parameter through the four insertion primitives, which is how the specification threads it); observe() does its four TypeErrors and the implied-option rules, on *presence* rather than truth, so {attributeOldValue: false} still watches attributes; removeAttribute of an absent attribute is no longer a mutation; inserting a fragment queues the record its own observers are owed for being emptied. Node.normalize() did not exist at all and now does -- iterative with an explicit stack, because the depth is a page's tree depth.

**The ordering inside a replacement is observable, and WPT is where it was pinned down.** The incoming node leaves its old parent *before* the outgoing child is removed, and that removal keeps its own record. `parent.replaceChild(parent.lastChild, parent.firstChild)` must report the last child leaving while the first is still beside it, and `parent.replaceChild(x, x)` must report a removal and then an insertion rather than one record replacing x with itself; the spec's note "the above can only be false if child is node" only parses under that order.

**The instrument grew: --verbose now prints the subtests behind a non-OK harness.** The expectation format still records one line for a timeout -- what is behind one is not yet a fact -- but a session diagnosing 85 of them could read "23 of 38 passed" in the summary and nothing about the fifteen. Every cause above came off that list. Same argument the harness-message line won a session ago.

**What is left, measured.** (1) `Attr` as a real node -- and part of it landed straight after, which is what says what the rest costs. attributes.js's `attributes_are`, the helper a third of attributes.html runs through, checks `attr.textContent` and `attr.ownerElement` on every attribute, and the record this browser handed back had neither; twenty lines added `textContent` and made `ownerElement` an *accessor* that re-asks the element whether it still carries the attribute, which is **+24 subtests in dom/nodes** and a green Attr-prefix.html. What is left of it is the design rather than the addition: identity (`el.attributes[0] === el.getAttributeNode('x')` is false here and true everywhere else), a `value` that writes through, and setAttributeNode / removeAttributeNode / createAttribute with InUseAttributeError. All three want one thing -- a table of materialised Attrs on the element's wrapper plus a detach at every attribute removal and replacement -- and that table wants two or three new members on DomBindings, which has no header lines left. It is the first work the class split is blocking rather than merely embarrassing. (2) The Range mutation methods (insertNode, deleteContents, extractContents, surroundContents) are seven of the eleven remaining failures in MutationObserver-childList, and they are **C5**, not C4. (3) innerHTML/outerHTML still queue two records where the DOM queues one (MutationObserver-inner-outer.html names all three subtests); the fix is the same "replace all" this session built for replaceChildren and textContent, but InsertParsedHtml makes its fragment internally so the caller cannot see the added nodes, and DomBindings.h had no line left to widen it with -- it is a one-parameter change on the far side of the class split that header has now deferred five times.

**The 85% target is not reachable without J1 and should be revised with that reason.** 390 of Document-createElementNS.html's 400 subtests, all 98 of Document-createElement.html's, the 654 across the two Document-characterSet-normalization files and roughly twenty-five .xhtml/.svg files run inside an <iframe> or in an XML document. processing-instruction-attributes.html's 136 are a WICG proposal and are not a gap in this browser either. What is left that C4 itself owns is (1) above.

tasks.title: nested browsing contexts
tasks.scope: ADR 0027: a browsing-context tree, contentDocument/contentWindow for a same-origin child, frames/parent/top, iframe loading, and the cross-origin WindowProxy -- from the first commit, not as a later hardening pass.
tasks.check: dom/ >= 90%, and the seven iframe-driven dom/ranges files report instead of timing out.
tasks.notes:
**Measured 2026-08-11, and it is the only route to dom/ at 90%.** dom/ is at 83.1% (35,899 of 43,207). 2,280 subtests are visibly failing and fixing *every one of them* reaches 88.4%; the other ~5,028 are behind 208 tests whose harness never reported. **~4,176 of those are seven files** -- Range-{cloneContents,deleteContents,extractContents,insertNode,surroundContents,set,compareBoundaryPoints}.html -- each driven entirely by iframe.onload over two <iframe>s, with every assertion inside an async_test that never starts. Another 498 are Document-createElement{,NS}.html, also iframes and also XML documents (src/xml landed with C9, so the parser exists). A stub does not pay here: those tests mutate iframe.contentDocument and call iframe.contentWindow.run(), so they need a fully scriptable same-origin child. The hard part is not rendering -- src/engine's Page is 16,000 lines that all assume there is exactly one document, which is what ADR 0027 s1 means by making Page a tree.

**2026-08-12, first half landed.** The frame *lifecycle* is in: a script-appended `<iframe>` loads, `iframe.src = other` re-navigates, `srcdoc` parses inline, a 404 still fires `load`, and `load` fires from a *task* rather than from where the document was set -- which is the ordering the whole feature turns on, see docs/session-log.md. **31 `dom/` tests went TIMEOUT -> OK.** What is left is TD-0059 and it is the larger half: `js::Interpreter` has one global and one set of intrinsics, so `contentWindow` is a plain object with a `.document`, the child's scripts never run, and `parent`/`top`/`postMessage` are absent. The seven `Range-*.html` files this check names call `iframe.contentWindow.run()`, so they need the realm rather than more lifecycle.

**2026-08-12, the realm landed (ADR 0042).** `js::Interpreter` now holds up to 64 realms, each with its own global, global scope and `js::Intrinsics`; a callable records its realm and the running realm follows the *callee*, so a builtin allocates from the realm its function came from. Nine tests in `tests/JsRealmTests.cpp`, +2.9% on the JS microbenchmarks recorded as TD-0060, and zero WPT regressions (dom/nodes/ re-run against a genuine pre-realm build). **What is left is the host half, and ADR 0042 §5 is the design plus the one hazard that dominates it**: `PageScript` owns an interpreter per `Page`, a same-origin child must borrow its parent's, and every one of ~40 host entry points must then run in the child's realm -- a missed one is a same-origin escape, not a bug, because the child's script would see the embedder's `window`. §5 says to build a realm-bound handle whose `operator->` carries the guard rather than to add `RealmScope` at 40 sites, and why. Do not start this without reading it.

tasks.notes: Compiles lazily where RunListenersOn already asks for the on<type> property -- HTML's internal raw uncompiled handler -- so there is no parser hook. Two things a next session must not undo. (1) csp::Policy::AllowsInlineHandler is its own function, not AllowsInline with two empty strings: the nonce-cancels-unsafe-inline rule is about <script> ELEMENTS, which can carry a nonce, and an attribute cannot -- so `script-src 'unsafe-inline' 'nonce-abc'` permits a handler while refusing an un-nonced inline script. (2) The compile is CAPPED at 10,000 per document, because Interpreter::Run calls BeginHostTurn (resetting the step budget) and retains the AST: a loop that rewrites the attribute and dispatches would refresh the budget metering it, which is a hang a page can drive. The gate crosses into src/bindings as a flag and defaults to deny. An inline event handler is what CSP 'unsafe-inline' governs, and src/bindings cannot see src/csp -- its allow: line is a security boundary (ADR 0008) and DocumentPolicy::AllowsInline lives in src/engine. So the gate is a flag the engine sets on the binding layer, the same inversion GeometrySource and NetworkSource use, and it is one boolean per document: nonces and hashes do not apply to handlers, only 'unsafe-inline' does (script-src-attr falling back to script-src). Landing the compilation without that flag opens a script-execution path CSP does not see.

tasks.notes:
Baseline 2026-08-10: 1.8%. importScripts is not defined; 200 of 284 tests time out on it, and it is 1,380 timeouts suite-wide.

**2026-08-14: the cause was not importScripts, it was that a worker had no global scope at all.** `engine::Workers` had owned a thread and a heap since session 38 and every test of it passed; what a script in that heap could *see* was `postMessage`, `self`, `name` and `onmessage`. `src/engine/WorkerScope.{h,cpp}` is the surface. Four things had to be true before one worker test could report: `self instanceof DedicatedWorkerGlobalScope` (testharness.js decides its environment with exactly that expression and otherwise concludes it is in a *shell*, which has no channel to report on), `importScripts` blocking the worker thread on the main loop, timers on the worker's own thread, and `addEventListener` declared as a bare global as well as on `self`.

Two bugs found on the way. Every worker message was delivered **twice** -- `DeliverWorkerMessage` called the `onmessage` property and then `dispatchEvent`, which runs `on<type>` again as the specification's implicit listener. And both test tools drove the engine as `if (Advance() || HasRunnableWork()) continue;` with `RunDueWork()` only on the else, while `RunDueWork` is what drains a worker's outbox and `HasRunnableWork` is true precisely when there is something in it. The same shape had already been found once in tools/snapshot for timers.

The API surface cost almost nothing: `URL`, `URLSearchParams`, `TextEncoder`, `atob`, `crypto`, `Blob`, `fetch`, `Headers`, `Request`, `Response`, `FormData`, `AbortController` and `XMLHttpRequest` in a worker are the *page's* implementations, because `DomBindings::document_` was already a pointer and `bindings::NetworkSource` was already an interface. **`src/url` is safe to call from a second thread and `src/dom` is not** -- one is a pure parser over generated const tables, the other has a process-wide intern table. Check that property before reaching for any other module from a worker.

What is left, in the order it blocks tests: `WebSocket` (20 of a 400-file sample's remaining harness errors; `websockets/` is 532 tests, and `bindings::SocketSource` is the same shape `NetworkSource` was), `IndexedDB` and `localStorage`, `OffscreenCanvas` (task F6, 889 tests). `SharedWorker` stays refused -- ADR 0022 §1 names it as the one thing the model exists to avoid.

**Worker results are load-sensitive** in a way the rest of the suite is not: a worker is a real second thread per test process. The same 400 files gave 4,215 passing subtests on an idle machine and 40 on the same binary while a build was running. Re-record at low concurrency and check the denominator.

tasks.title: an https origin in the harness
tasks.scope: A self-signed certificate trusted only by the runner, so the .https.html half of the suite runs at all.
tasks.notes:
**Done 2026-08-18.** The check ran and passed:

    $ microbrowser_wpt --jobs 3 FileAPI/historical.https.html
    1 tests in 56 ms: 11 subtests, 11 passed (100.0%), 0 crashes, 0 timeouts

`tools/wpt/Certificate.cpp` generates a P-256 CA and one leaf per run; the server binds two more ports and speaks TLS on them through the same poll loop; `{{ports[https][N]}}`, `{{location[scheme]}}` and `{{location[server]}}` answer with the real thing. **1,268 files in scope carry `.https.` in their name** (not 612 -- that figure counted only the Firefox gap) and every one of them now loads over TLS.

**Trust scoping**: the key pair is in memory, per run, valid a day; the CA private key never touches disk (the server is forked and inherits it); only the CA *certificate* is written to a temp file, because `SocketTransportFactory::Options::ca_bundle_path` takes a path, and it is removed when the run ends. Trust is installed by the tool through the existing `Loader::SetTransport` seam -- `src/` gained nothing, and `SharedContext` loads that bundle *instead of* the system roots, so a test process trusts this one CA and nothing else. The leaf is `CA:FALSE`; `SSL_VERIFY_PEER` and `SSL_set1_host` are untouched, which is why the leaf carries the substitution table's own name list rather than a wildcard.

**Not re-recorded, deliberately.** Five other agents were re-recording areas from the same base and a re-record measures the binary it started with. The areas a follow-up must re-record, by `.https.` file count: `html/` 514, `content-security-policy/` 226, `upgrade-insecure-requests/` 197, `fetch/` 177, `cookies/` 45, `storage/` 38, `resource-timing/` 12, `workers/` 11, `svg/` 11, then the twelve areas with fewer than ten.

**What it moved, measured but not recorded.** `fetch/metadata/`: three tests went TIMEOUT -> OK, including two *non*-https ones -- `helper.sub.js` builds its origins from `{{ports[https][0]}}`, so the http tests were failing on a port nothing listened on. One went OK -> TIMEOUT and it is real: `generated/window-location.https.sub.html` now reaches a live secure origin and hangs on `window.open()` returning null (task J6). `upgrade-insecure-requests/` is unchanged at 0 of 1,000 subtests -- those tests now fail for the right reason, which is that the directive is not implemented.

tasks.title: the reftest gate
tasks.scope: Reftests in the ctest registration, which still passes --testharness-only. F9 recorded all 20,998 and the run takes 105 seconds, so cost is not what is holding it back: eight of them are intermittent across two runs of the same binary, and a gate that is a coin toss eight times is worse than one that does not run. Name the eight, decide each (a disabled= line with a reason, a fuzzy annotation upstream would accept, or a real fix), then drop --testharness-only.
tasks.check: `microbrowser_wpt --reftests-only` twice in a row, both 0 unexpected, and the ctest registration no longer passes --testharness-only.
tasks.notes:
**Done 2026-08-31.** `microbrowser_wpt --reftests-only` printed `20998 reftests: 8005 passed (38.1%), 706 of those with both pages blank` and `0 unexpected results` on two consecutive runs, exit 0 both times, and `--testharness-only` is gone from the ctest registration in CMakeLists.txt (the cap went 5400s -> 7200s with it: 5400 was the testharness half alone and had no headroom).

**The eight were nine, and seven of them were one bug in the *browser*.** This task's own notes said `css/css-text/text-spacing-trim/` was an `@font-face` "which this browser does not load". Every clause of that is wrong: the fonts are in the checkout, the server serves them, `@font-face` has worked since 9ba34ee, and `gfx.web_fonts_registered` reads 2 on every load. What varied was whether the registered face was ever *used*. `platform::SystemFontProvider` memoises what a font stack resolves to and dropped that cache only in `Load`, whose comment claims loading a face is "the only event that can" change an answer -- untrue since `@font-face` landed. So a page laid out before its font arrived cached `chws-font -> <the fallback>`, and the relayout the arriving font triggered asked the same question and got the same answer: the web font never applied at all, and whether it did was a race between the fetch and the first layout.

Found by rendering one page thirty times with `microbrowser_snapshot` and hashing the PPMs -- 28 one way, 2 the other -- then `-v` on one of each: `Text 8.0,27.0 w=24.0` against `Text 8.0,32.0 w=40.0` for the same text at the same size is a different *face*. 30 of 30 identical afterwards.

**The eighth was the runner**: `RenderPage` waited on `!IsDocumentLoading() && !HasInFlightScriptFetches()` and a font download is in neither -- `Engine::IsLoading` has a third clause. A reftest is two loads, so the font could arrive for one and not the other. Cost of waiting: 90.4s -> 91.0s over 20,998 tests.

**The ninth was the retry policy writing a coin toss down.** `finish()` re-ran a disagreement before *reporting* it but not before *writing it down*, so one flip of `css/css-transitions/render-blocking/no-transition-from-ua-to-blocking-stylesheet.html` during the recording run became its expectation -- a file that passes 150 of 150 in isolation. The guard is gone; cost is proportional to what moved (58 disagreements out of 20,998), not to the area.

7,963 -> 8,005 passing files. 102 expectation lines deleted, 14 added. `css/css-fonts/` moved and was re-recorded; the other thirteen areas whose tests load a web font were checked and are 0 unexpected. **`resource-timing/` is 6 unexpected and is not this task's** -- it is one of the seven areas unmeasured since the 2026-08-15 merge, and it is now inside a gate that runs both halves.
